summary: This is a theory paper in the statistical-physics-of-learning tradition that introduces a 'single-location regression' (SLR) task to explain, mechanistically, why softmax attention outperforms linear attention on retrieval-like problems. Its core results are clean and non-trivial: softmax provably attains the Bayes risk at the population level (satisfying a Nishimori condition) while linear attention provably falls short, and a replica-based finite-sample analysis shows the advantage persists at proportional sample complexity. The main limitations are the stylized nature of the model (single layer, no query vectors, synthetic Gaussian data), the non-rigorous status of the central finite-sample result, and a modest empirical footprint, but the claims are carefully scoped and positioning against prior/concurrent work is strong.
strengths: Well-motivated question grounded in a concrete empirical observation (softmax's systematic advantage on retrieval tasks, Fig. 1), addressed with a tractable and unifying probabilistic model that subsumes spiked- and max-SLR variants.

Genuinely informative theoretical results: Prop. 4.2 (softmax attains Bayes risk), Corollaries 4.1-4.4 characterizing which activation properties (non-vanishing mean, cross-token normalization) are necessary, and explicit asymptotic separations in signal strength ν and sequence length L.

Careful, honest calibration: the paper explicitly flags the replica method as non-rigorous, notes softmax is no longer Bayes-optimal at finite α, and states the absence of learnable query vectors as a limitation.

Thorough, fair related-work positioning, including delineation from closely related concurrent works (Dohmatob 2025, Barnfield et al. 2026, Dragutinović et al. 2025) and the sequence multi-index literature (Cui 2025, Troiani et al. 2025).

key_concerns.issue: The central finite-sample characterization (Result 5.1) is derived via the non-rigorous replica method under a replica-symmetry/manifold assumption, and is validated against what appears to be single-run simulations without reported seeds, error bars, or variance across draws of (k*, v*) and datasets.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report simulation results with multiple seeds and error bars (or concentration diagnostics) in Fig. 3, and either sketch the conditions under which replica symmetry is expected to hold here or provide numerical evidence (e.g., replicon stability) supporting it.

key_concerns.issue: The gap between the SLR model and real attention is large (single non-learnable attention head, no query vectors, no MLP, Gaussian tokens), so the extent to which the results explain softmax's empirical dominance in LLMs remains an inference rather than a demonstrated link.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least a small controlled experiment on a semi-realistic retrieval task (e.g., MQAR-style) comparing softmax vs. linear vs. softplus-kernel single layers to test whether the predicted ordering and the normalization mechanism transfer beyond the Gaussian model.

key_concerns.issue: Novelty rests substantially on existing sequence multi-index / order-parameter machinery; the incremental pieces (variable sequence length, softmax tractability, activation comparison) are valuable but should be more sharply delineated against Marion et al. 2025 and Cui 2025.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add an explicit 'what is new here vs. prior machinery' paragraph or table isolating the technical contributions that were not already available.

key_concerns.issue: The claim that the population analysis 'captures the performance efficiently attainable by one-pass SGD' relies on a manifold-invariance argument with acknowledged out-of-manifold local minima and no formal convergence proof.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: State this connection as a supported conjecture and provide additional numerical evidence (e.g., fraction of SGD runs converging to the on-manifold minimizer across dimensions/initializations).

questions_for_authors: How sensitive are the finite-sample predictions to the manifold/diagonal-order-parameter simplification, and do full (non-restricted) simulations at moderate D deviate from Result 5.1?

Does the predicted ordering (softmax > softplus-kernel > erf > linear) and the role of cross-token normalization survive when the token distribution is non-Gaussian or when a learnable query is added?
Can you quantify variance across seeds in Fig. 3, and does the excellent theory-simulation agreement hold across all ν or degrade in the 'hard phase' near the Bayes-optimal discontinuity?
How does the analysis change if L̄ (max length) grows with D, i.e., in a regime closer to long-context retrieval?
calibration_check: Claims are appropriately scoped: the title's subtitle explicitly localizes the 'statistical advantage' to single-location regression, and the paper repeatedly flags its non-rigorous and modeling limitations rather than overclaiming generality.

significance.justification: Offers a clean mechanistic explanation (Bayes-optimality, normalization) for a real empirical phenomenon that the ML-theory community would cite and build on, though the toy-model scope tempers broader impact.

novelty.justification: The softmax Bayes-optimality result, variable-length treatment, and activation-function taxonomy are new, but the analytical machinery is largely inherited from existing sequence multi-index work and parallels concurrent submissions.

rigor.justification: Population-level results are stated as propositions with proofs, and the claim-evidence link is careful; the finite-sample core result is explicitly non-rigorous (replica) with acknowledged gaps in the SGD-convergence argument.

statistical_soundness.justification: Numerical checks corroborate the asymptotic formulas, but the main text reports no seeds, error bars, or variance quantification, and the key finite-sample result rests on an unverified replica-symmetry assumption.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations (no query vectors, non-rigorous replica, loss of Bayes-optimality at finite α) are stated plainly and claims are consistently scoped to the studied model.

clarity.justification: Logical flow and problem framing are clear and the risk terminology is tabulated, but the method sections are notation-dense and several key formulas (Result 5.1, self-consistent equations) are hard to parse in the body.

structure_compliance.justification: Follows a standard, well-organized conference structure (intro, related work, model, population analysis, finite-sample analysis, computational remarks) at appropriate length.

reproducibility.justification: Data model, activations, risks, and optimization procedure are specified with appendices and a code statement; some numerical details (regularization grids, simulation seeds) are deferred and would benefit from fuller in-text specification.

related_work.justification: Prior and concurrent work on alternatives to softmax, retrieval tasks, and sequence multi-index methods is fairly and comprehensively discussed with clear contribution delineation.

figure_quality.justification: Captions indicate figures directly support the claims (Fig. 2 activation comparison vs. Bayes risk; Fig. 3 theory-vs-simulation across tasks/α), and Fig. 1 grounds the motivation, though missing error bars limit their evidentiary weight.

breadth_generality.justification: Evidence spans two task variants and several activations but only small synthetic settings (L up to 10, single layer, Gaussian tokens); the generality supporting broad claims about softmax is correspondingly narrow.

overall_recommendation.justification: A well-executed, honestly scoped theory contribution with clean core results that sits at borderline-accept, held back by a stylized model, a non-rigorous central result, and limited empirical breadth.
